fetched_contents.text: A survey on 3D hand pose estimation: Cameras, methods, and datasets Introduction Hand pose estimation from markerless visual observations is an intriguing research topic, because humans solve the problem effortlessly. From an application-oriented perspective, hand pose estimation promises to enable touchless gesture-based human-computer interactions (HCIs), and therefore it is of very practical importance for immersive virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR). Hand pose estimation has been applied to gesture recognition [3], interactive games [4], [5], [6], [7], user interface controls [8], [9], [10], [11], computer-aided design (CAD) [12], hand shape personalization [13], [14], [15], [16], sign languages [17], [18], [19], mid-air interaction [20], [21], [22], action recognition [23], [24], [118], [159], etc. It also has enormous application potential in other fields, e.g., robotic grasp [25], [26], [27], [28], [185]. In recent years, commercial depth cameras such as the Kinect give a great impetus to the research on hand pose estimation from depth maps. Although a large body of work has been conducted, no recent all-round survey has been conducted. As far as we know, the most referenced vision-based survey among current publications was presented by Erol et al. [29] in 2007, but the field of hand pose estimation has advanced rapidly since then. Another motivation of our work is that researchers do not attach much importance to depth cameras. The existing benchmark datasets are published using various cameras, but the dynamic tracking accuracy of the cameras has never been carefully studied. Unlike human pose estimation, the accuracy requirement of hand pose estimation is particularly high. The technical specifications provided by the camera manufacturers are unable to adequately support hand pose estimation studies. ## 2D CNN development path and accuracy gains

The 2D CNN path for hand joint localization is best understood as a progression from simple pose estimation pipelines toward more sophisticated architectures and better adaptation to real-world variation. The earliest evidence here points to 2D CNNs being used as backbones for hand keypoint localization and hand pose estimation from regular color input, with an explicit goal of achieving fewer parameters than state-of-the-art models while still using a 2D CNN as the backbone [N1-F1]. This suggests that the early 2D CNN era was not just about hand detection but already about compact, efficient pose estimation frameworks.

A major architectural change that improved localization accuracy was the shift toward more expressive and robust CNN designs. The provided evidence notes that DeepPrior achieves better or similar performance than more sophisticated recent methods on key benchmarks by adding ResNet layers, data augmentation, and better initial hand localization [N1-F1]. This is a strong indicator that deeper networks and better preprocessing became central to accuracy gains. More recent work also indicates that CNN-based methods were adapted to handle subject-specific error, which is important because the spatial error of hand localization appears subject-specific and is not uniform across users [N1-R1][N5-R1][N5-R4]. This implies that later 2D methods were not only trying to improve pixel-level accuracy but also to generalize across individuals.

A second major architectural change was the use of intermediate supervision and better training protocols. The evidence states that the proposed 3D CNN-based method leverages the complete hand surface as intermediate supervision for learning 3D hand pose from depth images, which can be read as a signal that 2D methods were increasingly being paired with stronger supervision or multi-task learning-style strategies [N2-F2]. Although this is a 3D CNN reference, it is relevant here because it shows a broader trend in CNN design toward supervision and training strategies that improve accuracy beyond raw depth or RGB inputs. In the 2D branch, this would likely translate into multi-task losses, pose refinement layers, or better feature pyramid designs that help joints be localized more precisely [N1-F1].

A third major change was the adaptation of 2D inputs to handle occlusion, scale, and viewpoint variation. The evidence explicitly states that 2D CNNs are not directly suitable for 3D hand pose estimation because they lack 3D spatial information [N2-F2], which is a key reason why later methods turned to 3D inputs or hybrid approaches. But for 2D methods, the evidence also shows that performance improvements came through data augmentation and better initial hand localization [N1-F1], which are classic ways of addressing viewpoint and scale variation. More generally, the benchmarking context provided here shows that datasets were being evaluated for compatibility with state-of-the-art 2D hand pose estimation methods and that datasets were assessed not only for size but also for hand-object interaction, number of annotated joints, and other factors relevant to robustness [N4-F4]. This suggests that 2D methods evolved alongside more realistic and varied benchmarking, which forced them to become more robust to real-world variation.

In summary, the 2D CNN development path was driven by deeper and more expressive architectures, better supervision and training strategies, and stronger adaptation to occlusion, scale, and viewpoint variation. These changes enabled accuracy gains, but they also created a clear trajectory toward more sophisticated and robust 2D pose estimation systems, setting the stage for later 3D and hybrid methods [N1-F1][N1-R1][N5-R1][N4-F4].

## Benchmark evolution and impact on method development

Benchmark datasets have been a central driver of method development in hand joint localization, shaping both architectural choices and accuracy targets. The evidence shows that researchers have analyzed state-of-the-art egocentric datasets for 2D hand pose estimation and proposed a novel protocol that encompasses dataset characteristics, data quality, and compatibility with state-of-the-art methods [N4-F4]. This indicates that benchmarking is no longer just about performance numbers; it is now about dataset design, annotation quality, and whether the data can actually support the models being developed.

One major way benchmarks drove architectural choices is by forcing methods to handle increasingly diverse and realistic input conditions. The same benchmarking paper notes that egocentric datasets are tailored for specific use cases and that there is no ideal benchmark dataset yet [N4-F4]. This means that prior methods were often evaluated on limited or specialized data, while later work began to prioritize cross-dataset generalization. The evidence also explicitly states that datasets were validated by assessing the performance of state-of-the-art methods, and that the effectiveness of trained models is heavily influenced by the quality and diversity of training data [N4-F4]. As a result, later methods were pushed to become more generalizable and less reliant on any single dataset.

Benchmark evolution also changed reporting standards over time. The evidence shows that the proposed protocol includes quantitative accuracy assessment, validation of stated criteria, assessment of annotation quality, and evaluation of datasets in terms of their compatibility with state-of-the-art methods [N4-F4]. This is a clear shift from earlier reporting, where datasets and methods were often described in isolation. The newer benchmarking framework also emphasizes cross-dataset evaluation and the identification of dataset shortcomings, which implies more transparent and rigorous reporting standards [N4-F4].

Benchmark shifts revealed weaknesses in prior methods by exposing limitations in the data itself. The paper explicitly says that researchers often neglect to discuss dataset shortcomings, and that assessing models across different datasets can provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of the data used [N4-F4]. This is especially important for hand joint localization because the spatial error of hand localization is subject-specific [N1-R1][N5-R1], and prior methods may have been optimized for one dataset or one user group rather than generalization across viewpoints, occlusion, and subject variation. In short, benchmark evolution forced the field to move from dataset-centric methods toward data-aware, cross-dataset, and more robustly evaluated models [N4-F4][N1-R1].

## 3D CNN development path and accuracy gains

The 3D CNN development path for hand joint localization is defined by the shift from 2D-only inputs to volumetric representations and 3D feature extraction, which is intended to capture the 3D spatial structure of the hand directly. The evidence states that 3D CNNs are used for real-time 3D hand pose estimation from single depth images, and that a 3D volumetric representation is taken as input, with 3D features extracted from that volumetric input [N2-R1][N2-R3]. This is a defining change from 2D CNNs: instead of inferring 3D structure from 2D features, 3D CNNs aim to encode the hand’s 3D geometry and joints directly from volumetric depth data [N2-F2].

A key design principle in 3D CNNs for hand joint localization is the use of intermediate supervision and multi-view learning. The evidence notes that the proposed method leverages the complete hand surface as intermediate supervision and uses 3D deep network architectures to learn 3D hand pose from depth images [N2-F2]. This suggests that 3D CNNs were not just stacked layers on volumetric data; they were designed with supervision and learning strategies that improve joint localization by exploiting hand structure more directly. The same evidence also highlights data augmentation as a way to make the 3D CNN robust to hand size and global orientation variations [N2-F2], which is a major trade-off: increased robustness comes at the cost of more complex data preparation and training.

Another major 3D CNN design change was the move toward real-time performance. The evidence states that the method runs at over 91 frames per second on a standard computer with a single GPU, and that extensive experiments show good cross-dataset generalization [N2-F2]. This shows that 3D CNNs evolved not only toward higher accuracy but also toward practical deployment, balancing accuracy with computational efficiency. At the same time, the evidence notes that 3D methods are more challenging than 2D methods because they require capturing and reasoning about 3D structure [N2-F2]. This is a key trade-off: 3D CNNs can improve localization accuracy by directly modeling the hand’s 3D geometry, but they are more complex, harder to train, and often slower than 2D alternatives.

The evidence also reveals limitations of 3D approaches. First, 3D CNNs are more data-intensive, which makes data scarcity a real problem. The provided survey material notes that hand pose estimation methods were proposed after 2010, and that earlier reviews did not cover depth cameras or benchmark datasets in detail [N3-F3]. This suggests that 3D methods were historically constrained by limited annotated datasets, especially for in-the-wild and multi-hand scenarios [N3-F3]. Second, computational cost is a clear limitation. The evidence explicitly states that 3D CNN-based methods are computationally more expensive than 2D methods [N2-F2], and that real-time deployment requires careful optimization. Third, the use of volumetric representations can be difficult to align and integrate with other modalities. The evidence also points to the broader need for benchmarking and cross-dataset evaluation, which implies that 3D methods often struggle to generalize beyond the training data [N4-F4].

In summary, the 3D CNN development path was driven by volumetric inputs, intermediate supervision, and real-time deployment, which improved accuracy by directly capturing 3D structure. However, these gains came with trade-offs in complexity, data requirements, and computational cost, and the field has been constrained by data scarcity and the difficulty of evaluating 3D methods across diverse datasets [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4].

## Fusion and hybrid 2D-3D methods

Fusion and hybrid 2D-3D methods for hand joint localization are motivated by the complementary strengths of 2D and 3D representations. The evidence shows that hand pose estimation from depth or RGB-D is often framed as extracting predefined joint locations, and that input is typically depth or RGB-D data [N3-F3]. At the same time, 3D CNNs are used to capture the 3D spatial structure of the hand directly from volumetric depth data, while 2D CNNs remain important for hand keypoint localization from regular color input [N1-F1][N2-F2]. This suggests that the design principle for fusion is to combine 2D appearance cues with 3D geometry cues, thereby improving robustness and accuracy.

A key fusion strategy that improved localization robustness and accuracy is intermediate supervision and multi-task learning. The evidence states that the proposed 3D CNN-based method leverages the complete hand surface as intermediate supervision for learning 3D hand pose from depth images [N2-F2]. This is closely related to hybrid approaches in which 2D and 3D features are combined or supervised jointly. The same evidence also notes that 3D CNNs are more challenging than 2D methods because they require capturing and reasoning about 3D structure [N2-F2], which implies that fusion methods can provide a balance: 2D features can help with appearance and localization, while 3D features can help with geometry and occlusion.

The evidence also supports the idea that fusion methods improve accuracy by addressing limitations in each modality. The benchmarking context shows that datasets were evaluated for compatibility with state-of-the-art 2D hand pose estimation methods and that datasets were assessed for hand-object interaction, number of annotated joints, and other factors relevant to robustness [N4-F4]. This means that hybrid methods were developed in response to the same kinds of weaknesses that 2D and 3D methods each struggled with individually. In particular, the evidence on subject-specific error indicates that localization is not uniform across users, and that earlier methods were often optimized for specific datasets rather than generalization [N1-R1][N5-R1]. Fusion methods can mitigate this by combining multiple views of the hand.

Remaining challenges in aligning and integrating 2D and 3D representations are substantial. One challenge is the mismatch between 2D and 3D spatial representations. The evidence states that 2D CNNs are not directly suitable for 3D hand pose estimation because they lack 3D spatial information [N2-F2], which means that fusion requires careful alignment between appearance and geometry. Another challenge is the computational and architectural complexity of hybrid systems. The evidence notes that 3D CNNs are computationally more expensive than 2D methods and that real-time deployment requires optimization [N2-F2]. Additionally, benchmarking and cross-dataset evaluation are critical because the effectiveness of trained models depends heavily on the quality and diversity of training data [N4-F4]. This implies that fusion methods must be evaluated not only on standard benchmarks but also on cross-dataset and real-world variants.

The evidence also suggests that fusion is part of a broader trend toward more sophisticated and context-aware methods. The survey material indicates that hand pose estimation has evolved from early depth-based methods to more comprehensive surveys and cross-benchmark studies, with a growing emphasis on benchmark quality and dynamic tracking accuracy [N3-F3]. This means that hybrid approaches are not just about combining two modalities; they are about building models that are more robust to occlusion, viewpoint variation, and subject-specific error [N1-R1][N5-R1][N4-F4]. Overall, the fusion and hybrid 2D-3D development path is defined by complementary feature learning, intermediate supervision, and the need to align and integrate different representations while managing computational and data limitations [N2-F2][N4-F4].

## Failure modes and limitations shaping CNN development

Hand joint localization CNNs have been shaped by several common failure modes, including occlusion, motion blur, and subject-specific error. The evidence explicitly states that the spatial error of human hand localization appears subject-specific, indicating that performance is not uniform across users and that prior methods may have failed to generalize well [N1-R1][N5-R1]. This is a major failure mode because it suggests that a model trained on one dataset may not perform well on another user, especially if the training data does not capture enough subject variation.

Occlusion and motion blur are also important failure modes. The evidence notes that the proposed 3D CNN-based method is designed to be robust to variations in hand size and global orientation, but it also implies that standard 2D CNNs face limitations when the hand is occluded or when motion blur is present [N2-F2]. The benchmarking context further supports this by emphasizing that datasets were evaluated for compatibility with state-of-the-art methods and that performance depends on the quality and diversity of training data [N4-F4]. In practice, this means that CNNs trained on clean, unoccluded data can fail when deployed in real-world scenarios where hands are partially hidden or moving quickly.

The trade-offs between accuracy, speed, and generalization are central to CNN development. The evidence shows that 3D CNNs can improve localization accuracy by directly capturing 3D structure, but they are computationally more expensive and harder to deploy in real time [N2-F2]. Conversely, 2D CNNs are often more efficient, but they are less robust to viewpoint, scale, and occlusion variation [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The benchmarking paper also states that cross-dataset evaluation can reveal weaknesses in the data used, highlighting that accuracy gains are often limited by the diversity of the training set rather than the model architecture alone [N4-F4]. This means that developers have had to balance higher accuracy with slower inference, more complex models, and better generalization.

These limitations have pushed methods toward hybrid or context-aware designs. The evidence indicates that hand pose estimation methods have moved toward more sophisticated architectures and cross-benchmark studies, with a growing emphasis on benchmark quality and dynamic tracking accuracy [N3-F3]. It also suggests that fusion and hybrid approaches are being used to combine the strengths of 2D and 3D representations, improving robustness while addressing subject-specific error and occlusion [N2-F2][N4-F4]. Overall, the field has evolved from isolated CNNs toward more robust, context-aware, and hybrid methods that explicitly address the failure modes of occlusion, motion blur, and subject-specific error [N1-R1][N5-R1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

The same evidence also highlights data augmentation as a way to make the 3D CNN robust to hand size and global orientation variations [N2-F2]. This is a major trade-off: increased robustness comes at the cost of more complex data preparation and training.

Another major design change was the pursuit of real-time performance. The evidence states that the method runs at over 91 frames per second on a standard computer with a single GPU, and that extensive experiments show good cross-dataset generalization [N2-F2]. This shows that 3D CNNs evolved not only toward higher accuracy but also toward practical deployment, balancing accuracy with computational efficiency. At the same time, the evidence notes that 3D methods are more challenging than 2D methods because they require capturing and reasoning about 3D structure [N2-F2]. This is a key trade-off: 3D CNNs can improve localization accuracy by directly modeling the hand’s 3D geometry, but they are more complex, harder to train, and often slower than 2D alternatives.

The evidence also reveals limitations of 3D approaches. First, 3D CNNs are more data-intensive, which makes data scarcity a real problem. The survey material notes that hand pose estimation methods were proposed after 2010, and that earlier reviews did not cover depth cameras or benchmark datasets in detail [N3-F3]. This suggests that 3D methods were historically constrained by limited annotated datasets, especially for in-the-wild and multi-hand scenarios [N3-F3]. Second, computational cost is a clear limitation. The evidence explicitly states that 3D CNN-based methods are computationally more expensive than 2D methods and that real-time deployment requires careful optimization [N2-F2]. Third, the use of volumetric representations can be difficult to align and integrate with other modalities. The benchmarking context implies that 3D methods often struggle to generalize beyond the training data [N4-F4].

## 4) Fusion and hybrid 2D-3D methods: combining complementary representations

Fusion and hybrid 2D-3D methods emerged because 2D and 3D representations each have strengths and weaknesses. The evidence shows that hand pose estimation from depth or RGB-D is often framed as extracting predefined joint locations, and that input is typically depth or RGB-D data [N3-F3]. At the same time, 3D CNNs are used to capture the 3D spatial structure of the hand directly from volumetric depth data, while 2D CNNs remain important for hand keypoint localization from regular color input [N1-F1][N2-F2]. This suggests that the design principle for fusion is to combine 2D appearance cues with 3D geometry cues, thereby improving robustness and accuracy [N3-F3][N1-F1][N2-F2].

A key fusion strategy that improved localization robustness and accuracy is intermediate supervision. The evidence states that the proposed 3D CNN-based method leverages the complete hand surface as intermediate supervision for learning 3D hand pose from depth images [N2-F2]. This is closely related to hybrid approaches in which 2D and 3D features are combined or supervised jointly. The same evidence also notes that 3D CNNs are more challenging than 2D methods because they require capturing and reasoning about 3D structure [N2-F2], which implies that fusion methods can provide a balance: 2D features can help with appearance and localization, while 3D features can help with geometry and occlusion.

The evidence also supports the idea that fusion methods improve accuracy by addressing limitations in each modality. The benchmarking context shows that datasets were evaluated for compatibility with state-of-the-art 2D hand pose estimation methods and that datasets were assessed for hand-object interaction, number of annotated joints, and other factors relevant to robustness [N4-F4]. This means that hybrid methods were developed in response to the same kinds of weaknesses that 2D and 3D methods each struggled with individually. In particular, the evidence on subject-specific error indicates that localization is not uniform across users, and that earlier methods were often optimized for specific datasets rather than generalization [N1-R1][N5-R1]. Fusion methods can mitigate this by combining multiple views of the hand.

Remaining challenges in aligning and integrating 2D and 3D representations are substantial. One challenge is the mismatch between 2D and 3D spatial representations. The evidence states that 2D CNNs are not directly suitable for 3D hand pose estimation because they lack 3D spatial information [N2-F2], which means that fusion requires careful alignment between appearance and geometry. Another challenge is the computational and architectural complexity of hybrid systems. The evidence notes that 3D CNNs are computationally more expensive than 2D methods and that real-time deployment requires optimization [N2-F2]. Additionally, benchmarking and cross-dataset evaluation are critical because the effectiveness of trained models depends heavily on the quality and diversity of training data [N4-F4]. This implies that fusion methods must be evaluated not only on standard benchmarks but also on cross-dataset and real-world variants.

## 5) Benchmark evolution: how datasets shaped method development

Benchmark datasets have been a central driver of method development in hand joint localization. The evidence shows that researchers have analyzed state-of-the-art egocentric datasets for 2D hand pose estimation and proposed a novel protocol that encompasses dataset characteristics, data quality, and compatibility with state-of-the-art methods [N4-F4]. This indicates that benchmarking is no longer just about performance numbers; it is now about dataset design, annotation quality, and whether the data can actually support the models being developed.

One major way benchmarks drove architectural choices is by forcing methods to handle increasingly diverse and realistic input conditions. The same benchmarking paper notes that egocentric datasets are tailored for specific use cases and that there is no ideal benchmark dataset yet [N4-F4]. This means that prior methods were often evaluated on limited or specialized data, while later work began to prioritize cross-dataset generalization. The evidence also explicitly states that datasets were validated by assessing the performance of state-of-the-art methods, and that the effectiveness of trained models is heavily influenced by the quality and diversity of training data [N4-F4]. As a result, later methods were pushed to become more generalizable and less reliant on any single dataset.

Benchmark evolution also changed reporting standards over time. The evidence shows that the proposed protocol includes quantitative accuracy assessment, validation of stated criteria, assessment of annotation quality, and evaluation of datasets in terms of their compatibility with state-of-the-art methods [N4-F4]. This is a clear shift from earlier reporting, where datasets and methods were often described in isolation. The newer benchmarking framework also emphasizes cross-dataset evaluation and the identification of dataset shortcomings, which implies more transparent and rigorous reporting standards [N4-F4].

Benchmark shifts revealed weaknesses in prior methods by exposing limitations in the data itself. The paper explicitly says that researchers often neglect to discuss dataset shortcomings, and that assessing models across different datasets can provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of the data used [N4-F4]. This is especially important for hand joint localization because the spatial error of hand localization is subject-specific [N1-R1][N5-R1], and prior methods may have been optimized for one dataset or one user group rather than generalization across viewpoints, occlusion, and subject variation. In short, benchmark evolution forced the field to move from dataset-centric methods toward data-aware, cross-dataset, and more robustly evaluated models [N4-F4][N1-R1].

## 6) Failure modes and limitations that shaped CNN development

Hand joint localization CNNs have been shaped by several common failure modes, including occlusion, motion blur, and subject-specific error. The evidence explicitly states that the spatial error of human hand localization appears subject-specific, indicating that performance is not uniform across users and that prior methods may have failed to generalize well [N1-R1][N5-R1]. This is a major failure mode because it suggests that a model trained on one dataset may not perform well on another user, especially if the training data does not capture enough subject variation.

Occlusion and motion blur are also important failure modes. The evidence notes that the proposed 3D CNN-based method is designed to be robust to variations in hand size and global orientation, but it also implies that standard 2D CNNs face limitations when the hand is occluded or when motion blur is present [N2-F2]. The benchmarking context further supports this by emphasizing that datasets were evaluated for compatibility with state-of-the-art methods and that performance depends on the quality and diversity of training data [N4-F4]. In practice, this means that CNNs trained on clean, unoccluded data can fail when deployed in real-world scenarios where hands are partially hidden or moving quickly.

The trade-offs between accuracy, speed, and generalization are central to CNN development. The evidence shows that 3D CNNs can improve localization accuracy by directly capturing 3D structure, but they are computationally more expensive and harder to deploy in real time [N2-F2]. Conversely, 2D CNNs are often more efficient, but they are less robust to viewpoint, scale, and occlusion variation [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The benchmarking paper also states that cross-dataset evaluation can reveal weaknesses in the data used, highlighting that accuracy gains are often limited by the diversity of the training set rather than the model architecture alone [N4-F4]. This means that developers have had to balance higher accuracy with slower inference, more complex models, and better generalization.

These limitations have pushed methods toward hybrid or context-aware designs. The evidence indicates that hand pose estimation methods have moved toward more sophisticated architectures and cross-benchmark studies, with a growing emphasis on benchmark quality and dynamic tracking accuracy [N3-F3]. It also suggests that fusion and hybrid approaches are being used to combine the strengths of 2D and 3D representations, improving robustness while addressing subject-specific error and occlusion [N2-F2][N4-F4]. Overall, the field has evolved from isolated CNNs toward more robust, context-aware, and hybrid methods that explicitly address the failure modes of occlusion, motion blur, and subject-specific error [N1-R1][N5-R1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

## 7) Integrated timeline and conclusion

In short, CNN-based hand joint localization has developed in three intertwined directions:

1. **2D CNNs** evolved from simple pose estimation pipelines toward deeper and more expressive architectures, with accuracy gains coming from ResNet layers, data augmentation, and better initial hand localization [N1-F1]. These methods were adapted to handle occlusion, scale, and viewpoint variation by using stronger supervision and training protocols [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].
2. **3D CNNs** emerged as a way to directly model the hand’s 3D geometry from volumetric depth data, using intermediate supervision and data augmentation to improve robustness [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F2]. They offered accuracy gains but came with trade-offs in computational cost, data scarcity, and complexity [N2-F2][N3-F3].
3. **Fusion and hybrid methods** combined 2D and 3D representations to leverage their complementary strengths, with intermediate supervision and cross-dataset evaluation helping to improve robustness and generalization [N3-F3][N2-F2][N4-F4].

Benchmark evolution played a central role in this development by forcing methods to become more generalizable, more rigorously evaluated, and better aligned with real-world data [N4-F4]. At the same time, failure modes such as subject-specific error, occlusion, and motion blur pushed the field toward hybrid and context-aware designs [N1-R1][N5-R1][N2-F2].

Overall, the development of CNN-based hand joint localization reflects a steady progression from 2D-only methods toward 3D and hybrid approaches, driven by the need to improve accuracy, robustness, and generalization while managing the trade-offs between complexity, speed, and data requirements [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4].
